stem:
An image is built from this Dockerfile and started with `docker run myapp` (no other flags). Can a browser on the host reach the app at `http://localhost:3000`?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

options.text: Yes, because `EXPOSE 3000` publishes container port 3000 on host port 3000
options.why: `EXPOSE` never publishes anything by itself; publishing happens at run time.

options.text: No, `EXPOSE` only documents the port; it must be published with `-p` or `-P`
options.why: EXPOSE is metadata for whoever runs the image. `-p 3000:3000` or `-P` actually maps a host port.

options.text: Yes, but only on Docker Desktop, which forwards every exposed port to localhost automatically
options.why: Docker Desktop forwards published ports, not merely exposed ones.

options.text: No, because `EXPOSE` needs an explicit protocol such as `3000/tcp` to take effect
options.why: TCP is the default protocol; the protocol has nothing to do with publishing.

explanation: `EXPOSE` is documentation between the image author and whoever runs the container. It does not open or map a port. To reach the app from the host, publish it with `docker run -p 3000:3000 myapp`, or use `-P` to map every exposed port to a random high host port.

stem: A Dockerfile can contain several `CMD` instructions, and when the container starts they run one after another in the order they appear.

options.text: True
options.why: Only one CMD is effective; earlier ones are overridden rather than chained.

options.text: False
options.why: If a Dockerfile lists more than one CMD, only the last one takes effect.

explanation: A Dockerfile has a single effective `CMD`: if several are listed, only the last one counts. `CMD` supplies the default command (or default arguments for `ENTRYPOINT`) for one process. To run several steps at start-up, use a script as the entrypoint.

stem:
What does the final `RUN pwd` print during the build?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine
WORKDIR /a
WORKDIR b
WORKDIR c
RUN pwd
```

options.text: `/c`, because each WORKDIR replaces the previous one
options.why: Relative WORKDIR paths are resolved against the previous WORKDIR, not the root.

options.text: `/`, because WORKDIR changes only apply to CMD and ENTRYPOINT
options.why: WORKDIR applies to RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY and ADD that follow it.
Each relative WORKDIR is joined onto the previous one.

options.text: The build fails, because `/a/b` and `/a/b/c` were never created with `mkdir`
options.why: WORKDIR creates the directory if it does not exist.

explanation: When `WORKDIR` gets a relative path, it is resolved against the previous `WORKDIR`, so `/a`, then `b`, then `c` gives `/a/b/c`. Missing directories are created automatically, even if no later instruction uses them.

stem: A valid Dockerfile must start with `FROM`, except for one instruction that may appear before it, for example to parameterise the base image tag. Type the name of that instruction.
explanation: `ARG` is the only instruction that may precede `FROM` (parser directives and comments aside). An `ARG` declared there can be used in `FROM` lines, such as `FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}`, but it sits outside every build stage.

stem: A teammate asks why the team style guide prefers `COPY` over `ADD` for files from the build context. Which difference between the two is correct?

options.text: `COPY` can only copy single files, while `ADD` can copy whole directories
options.why: Both copy files and directories from the context.

options.text: `ADD` auto-extracts a local tar archive and can fetch URLs; `COPY` just copies
options.why: That extra "magic" is why COPY is preferred when you only need a plain copy.

options.text: `COPY` always produces a smaller layer, because ADD stores a second compressed copy
options.why: Neither keeps an extra copy; layer size depends on the files copied.

options.text: `ADD` respects `.dockerignore`, while `COPY` ignores it and sees every file
options.why: `.dockerignore` filters the context itself, so it applies to both.

explanation: `ADD` does everything `COPY` does, plus it extracts local tar archives into the destination and can download remote URLs or clone Git repositories. Because a local `.tar.gz` silently becomes a directory with `ADD`, plain `COPY` is the clearer choice for ordinary files.

stem: Match each Dockerfile instruction with what it does.

options.text: Sets the executable that always runs when the container starts
options.why: ENTRYPOINT

options.text: Provides default arguments or a default command that `docker run` arguments replace
options.why: CMD

options.text: Tells Docker how to test whether the running container still works
options.why: HEALTHCHECK

options.text: Chooses the signal `docker stop` sends to the main process
options.why: STOPSIGNAL

explanation: `ENTRYPOINT` fixes the executable; `CMD` supplies defaults that are easy to override with arguments to `docker run`. `HEALTHCHECK` defines a probe whose exit code sets the health status, and `STOPSIGNAL` changes what `docker stop` sends (SIGTERM by default).

stem:
What does `AS build` add to this line?

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.24 AS build
```

options.text: It tags the final image as `build` when the build finishes
options.why: Image tags come from `docker build -t`, not from stage names.

options.text: It names the stage so later lines can use `COPY --from=build` or `FROM build`
options.why: Stage names are references inside the same Dockerfile.

options.text: It tells BuildKit to skip this stage entirely unless `--target build` is passed on the CLI
options.why: Stages needed by the target are built whatever their name.

options.text: It marks the stage as a builder whose files are removed from every layer
options.why: Naming does not change which files end up in an image.

explanation: `FROM <image> AS <name>` starts a new build stage and gives it a name. Later instructions can refer to it with `FROM build`, `COPY --from=build` or `RUN --mount=type=bind,from=build`. This is the basis of multi-stage builds, where only the final stage becomes the image.

stem: Which two statements about `.dockerignore` are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: It removes matching files from the build context before the context is sent to the builder
options.why: That keeps the context small and keeps files like `.env` out of COPY.

options.text: The client looks for it in the root directory of the build context
options.why: A Dockerfile-specific `<name>.dockerignore` next to the Dockerfile is the other option.

options.text: It also hides matching files that already exist in the base image
options.why: It only filters the local build context; the base image is untouched.

options.text: It is applied at `docker run` to stop files being mounted into containers
options.why: It plays no part at run time.

options.text: Its patterns are regular expressions, so `.*\.log` excludes every log file
options.why: Patterns use Go filepath.Match rules plus `**`, not regular expressions.

explanation: The build client reads `.dockerignore` from the root of the context, or a `<Dockerfile-name>.dockerignore` placed next to that Dockerfile. It drops matching paths before the context is sent, which speeds builds and stops secrets or `node_modules` reaching `COPY . .`. Patterns follow Go `filepath.Match` rules, with `**` for any number of directories.

stem:
The image below is started with `docker run myapp npm test`. What runs as the container's main process?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

options.text: `node server.js npm test`
options.why: There is no ENTRYPOINT, so the arguments are not appended to the CMD.

options.text: `npm test`
options.why: Without an ENTRYPOINT, arguments to `docker run` replace CMD entirely.

options.text: `node server.js`, then `npm test` after it exits
options.why: CMD is a single default command; Docker does not chain commands.

options.text: `/bin/sh -c "npm test"`, because run arguments always go through a shell
options.why: Run arguments are executed directly; no shell is added.

explanation: When an image has no `ENTRYPOINT`, its `CMD` is the default command, and anything after the image name in `docker run` replaces it. So `npm test` runs instead of `node server.js`.

stem:
The image is started with `docker run api --port 9000`. Which command runs?

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.13-slim
COPY app.py .
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]
CMD ["--port", "80"]
```

options.text: `python app.py --port 80 --port 9000`
options.why: Run arguments replace CMD; they are not appended after it.

options.text: `--port 9000`, which fails because it is not an executable
options.why: With an ENTRYPOINT set, run arguments become its arguments.

options.text: `python app.py --port 9000`
options.why: CMD only supplies default arguments, which the run arguments replace.

options.text: `python app.py --port 80`, because CMD in exec form cannot be overridden
options.why: Exec-form CMD is overridden exactly like any other CMD.

explanation: With an exec-form `ENTRYPOINT`, the final command is the `ENTRYPOINT` array followed by the arguments. Those arguments come from `CMD` by default, but `docker run` arguments replace `CMD`. This pattern gives a fixed executable with easy-to-change flags.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Understand how CMD and ENTRYPOINT interact)

stem:
The image builds, but the container exits at once with `/bin/sh: [node,: not found`. What is wrong?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
COPY server.js .
CMD ['node', 'server.js']
```

options.text: Alpine images have no `node` binary on the default PATH
options.why: The node:22-alpine image does put node on the PATH.

options.text: Single quotes are not valid JSON, so the line is run in shell form as literal text
options.why: Exec form must be a JSON array with double-quoted strings.

options.text: CMD in exec form needs a WORKDIR before it, or it starts from the wrong directory at runtime
options.why: The error shows the shell trying to run `[node,` as a command, not a path problem.

options.text: `server.js` must be copied with ADD for CMD to find it
options.why: COPY puts the file in the image just as well.

explanation: The exec form is parsed as a JSON array, so each word needs double quotes. `['node', 'server.js']` is not valid JSON, so the whole line is treated as shell form and handed to `/bin/sh -c`. The shell then tries to run `[node,`. Write `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Shell and exec form)

stem:
What does this build step print?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine
RUN ["echo", "$HOME"]
```

options.text: `/root`
options.why: That would need a shell to expand the variable.

options.text: An empty line, because HOME is not set during builds
options.why: Nothing expands the variable at all, set or not.

options.text: The build fails, because exec-form RUN does not allow `$` characters
options.why: Any string is allowed; it is just passed through unchanged.

options.text: The literal text `$HOME`
options.why: Exec form runs echo directly with no shell, so no expansion happens.

explanation: Exec form calls the program directly, without a shell, so shell processing such as `$VAR` expansion does not happen and `echo` prints `$HOME`. Use shell form (`RUN echo $HOME`) or call a shell explicitly (`RUN ["sh", "-c", "echo $HOME"]`).

stem:
After these instructions, what are the values of `def` and `ghi`?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine
ENV abc=hello
ENV abc=bye def=$abc
ENV ghi=$abc
```

options.text: `def=bye`, `ghi=bye`
options.why: Substitution inside one instruction uses the values from before that instruction.

options.text: `def=hello`, `ghi=bye`
options.why: The new `abc` only takes effect from the next instruction.

options.text: `def=hello`, `ghi=hello`
options.why: By the third line `abc` has already been changed to bye.

options.text: `def=$abc` and `ghi=$abc` as literal text
options.why: The builder expands variables in ENV values.

explanation: Environment substitution uses the same value for a variable throughout a whole instruction. In `ENV abc=bye def=$abc`, `$abc` still means `hello`, so `def=hello`. The next instruction sees `abc=bye`, so `ghi=bye`.

stem:
This Dockerfile is built with `docker build --build-arg CONT_IMG_VER=v2.0.1 .`. What does the RUN step print?

```dockerfile
FROM ubuntu
ARG CONT_IMG_VER
ENV CONT_IMG_VER=v1.0.0
RUN echo $CONT_IMG_VER
```

options.text: `v2.0.1`, because `--build-arg` overrides everything in the Dockerfile
options.why: A build arg only sets the ARG; a later ENV of the same name wins.

options.text: An empty string, because ARG values are hidden from RUN
options.why: ARG values are visible to RUN after the ARG line.
ENV always overrides an ARG of the same name.

options.text: The build fails, because a name cannot be both an ARG and an ENV
options.why: Using the same name is allowed; the ENV simply takes precedence.

explanation: Variables set with `ENV` always override an `ARG` of the same name, much like a local variable shadowing an argument. To let the build arg win, write `ENV CONT_IMG_VER=${CONT_IMG_VER:-v1.0.0}`, which uses the arg when given and falls back to the default.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Using ARG variables)

stem: An `ARG VERSION=1.36` declared before the first `FROM` can be read directly by a `RUN echo $VERSION` inside that stage, with no further declaration.

options.text: True
options.why: An ARG before FROM is outside every stage and is only usable in FROM lines.

options.text: False
options.why: The stage must re-declare it with `ARG VERSION` (no value) to read the value.

explanation: An `ARG` declared before the first `FROM` is outside every build stage, so it can only be used in `FROM` lines. To use its value inside a stage, add `ARG VERSION` with no value after the `FROM`; it then picks up the global default or the `--build-arg` value.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Understand how ARG and FROM interact)

stem:
Given this Dockerfile, which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
RUN useradd -m app
USER app
WORKDIR /home/app
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

options.text: `package.json` is owned by root, because COPY ignores USER unless `--chown` is used
options.why: Without `--chown`, COPY creates files with UID and GID 0.

options.text: `npm install` and the final `node index.js` both run as the `app` user
options.why: USER applies to later RUN instructions and to the runtime CMD/ENTRYPOINT.

options.text: `useradd` fails because USER is set before it runs
options.why: useradd runs before the USER line, still as root.

options.text: COPY creates `package.json` owned by `app` because USER was set first
options.why: COPY needs `--chown=app:app` to change ownership.

options.text: USER only affects the container at runtime; build steps always run as root
options.why: USER also sets the user for subsequent RUN instructions.

explanation: `USER` sets the user for the rest of the stage: later `RUN` steps and the runtime `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT`. `COPY` and `ADD` do not follow it. Without `--chown`, copied files belong to UID and GID 0, so use `COPY --chown=app:app package.json .` if the app user must write to them.

stem: Put these stages of `docker build -t app .` in the order they happen.

options.text: The client reads `.dockerignore` and filters the local context
The filtered build context is sent to the builder
The builder reads the `# syntax=` parser directive and loads that frontend
The frontend runs the Dockerfile instructions, starting from FROM

explanation: Filtering happens client-side, so ignored files never leave your machine. The builder then receives the context. The `# syntax=` directive at the top of the Dockerfile picks the frontend (the parser) that interprets the file, and that frontend executes the instructions.
reference: Docker docs: Build context; Custom Dockerfile syntax

stem: A `HEALTHCHECK` is declared with only `--interval=10s`. How many consecutive failed checks does it take, by default, before the container is marked `unhealthy`? Type a number.
explanation: The default `--retries` is 3, so three consecutive failures turn the status to `unhealthy`. The other defaults are interval 30s, timeout 30s, start-period 0s and start-interval 5s.

stem:
What ends up in the image after this line, assuming the URL serves a gzipped tarball?

```dockerfile
ADD https://example.com/tool-1.2.tar.gz /opt/
```

options.text: The archive is downloaded and extracted into `/opt/`
options.why: Remote archives are not extracted by default; only local tar archives are.

options.text: The file `/opt/tool-1.2.tar.gz`, downloaded but not extracted
options.why: Extraction of a remote archive needs `ADD --unpack`.

options.text: Nothing: ADD cannot fetch URLs when BuildKit is enabled
options.why: BuildKit supports URL sources for ADD.

options.text: A directory `/opt/tool-1.2.tar.gz/` holding the extracted files
options.why: The file is placed as-is, named from the URL path.

explanation: For a URL source, `ADD` downloads the file. With a destination ending in `/`, the file name comes from the URL path, and the file gets permissions 600. Remote archives are not extracted unless you use `ADD --unpack`. Only local tar archives are unpacked automatically.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (ADD, adding files from a URL)

stem:
`docker stop` on this container always waits the full 10 seconds and then kills it, so the app never runs its SIGTERM handler. Why?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT node server.js
```

options.text: Node.js ignores SIGTERM unless it runs with `--enable-signals`
options.why: Node receives SIGTERM normally when it is the process the signal is sent to.

options.text: The default STOPSIGNAL is SIGKILL, which cannot be handled
options.why: The default STOPSIGNAL is SIGTERM.

options.text: Shell form makes `/bin/sh -c` PID 1, and the shell doesn't forward SIGTERM to node
options.why: Use exec form: `ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]`.

options.text: WORKDIR must come after ENTRYPOINT for stop signals to reach the running process
options.why: Instruction order has no effect on signal delivery.

explanation: Shell form wraps the command in `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell is PID 1 and node is its child. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM to PID 1, the shell does not pass it on, and after the timeout Docker sends SIGKILL. Exec form makes node PID 1, so it gets the signal directly.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (ENTRYPOINT shell form)

stem:
The container is started with `docker run svc --verbose`. Which command runs?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT node server.js
CMD ["--debug"]
```

options.text: `/bin/sh -c "node server.js"`, without `--debug` or `--verbose`
options.why: Shell-form ENTRYPOINT ignores both CMD and run arguments.

options.text: `node server.js --verbose`
options.why: That is the exec-form behaviour; shell form drops the run arguments.

options.text: `node server.js --debug --verbose`
options.why: Run arguments never append to CMD, and shell form ignores both anyway.

options.text: `--verbose`, run as a command because run arguments replace ENTRYPOINT
options.why: Run arguments replace CMD, not ENTRYPOINT; `--entrypoint` replaces ENTRYPOINT.

explanation: A shell-form `ENTRYPOINT` becomes `/bin/sh -c "node server.js"`. It ignores `CMD` and any `docker run` arguments, so neither flag reaches node. To accept flags, use exec form: `ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]`.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Understand how CMD and ENTRYPOINT interact)

stem:
The base image `acme/base` defines `CMD ["--serve"]`. A child image adds only an entrypoint. With `docker run child`, what arguments does `/entry.sh` receive?

```dockerfile
FROM acme/base
COPY entry.sh /entry.sh
ENTRYPOINT ["/entry.sh"]
```

options.text: `--serve`, inherited from the base image
options.why: Setting ENTRYPOINT clears an inherited CMD.

options.text: None: setting ENTRYPOINT resets the inherited CMD to empty
options.why: CMD must be set again in the child image to keep default arguments.

options.text: `/bin/sh -c --serve`, since the inherited CMD is treated as shell form
options.why: The inherited CMD is dropped, not reinterpreted.

options.text: The build fails because a child cannot set ENTRYPOINT when the base has CMD
options.why: This is valid; it just changes the effective CMD.

explanation: If `CMD` comes from the base image, setting `ENTRYPOINT` resets `CMD` to empty. The child must declare `CMD ["--serve"]` again if it wants those default arguments. This often surprises people who expect base-image defaults to carry over.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (CMD and ENTRYPOINT note)

stem:
A build needs an npm token. Which two approaches leave the token recoverable by anyone who can pull the image? (Choose two.)

```dockerfile
# 1
ARG NPM_TOKEN
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc && npm ci && rm .npmrc

# 2
ENV NPM_TOKEN=abc123

# 3
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci
```

options.text: Approach 1: the ARG value can be seen with `docker history`
options.why: Build args are visible in history and provenance, even if the file is deleted later.

options.text: Approach 2: ENV values are stored in the image config
options.why: ENV persists into the image and every container started from it.

options.text: Approach 3: secret mounts are written into the layer and kept in the image
options.why: Secret mounts exist only while that RUN step runs and are not saved in any layer.

options.text: Approach 1 is safe because `rm .npmrc` removes the token from every layer
options.why: The ARG value is still recorded in the image history.

options.text: None of the approaches leak, because images are private by default
options.why: Anyone who can pull the image can inspect its history and config.

explanation: Build arguments appear in `docker history` and in max-mode provenance, so `ARG` must never carry secrets, even if the file is deleted in the same step. `ENV` values are stored in the image configuration. `RUN --mount=type=secret` exposes the secret only for that one step and never writes it to a layer.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (ARG warning, RUN --mount=type=secret)

stem:
With the default BuildKit builder, does `/data/seed.txt` exist in the final image?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine
VOLUME /data
RUN echo hello > /data/seed.txt
```

options.text: No, because changes to a declared volume are always discarded
options.why: Discarding was the legacy builder's behaviour, not BuildKit's.

options.text: No, because `/data` is replaced by an empty anonymous volume during the build
options.why: No volume is mounted during a build.

options.text: The build fails, because RUN cannot write under a VOLUME path
options.why: Writing there is allowed.

options.text: Yes with BuildKit; the legacy builder would have discarded the change
options.why: The Dockerfile reference documents this difference between builders.

explanation: The reference notes that build steps changing data inside a declared volume were discarded by the legacy builder, while BuildKit keeps the change. For portable Dockerfiles, write the data before declaring `VOLUME`, or seed it at container start.

stem:
What do the two RUN steps print?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine AS base
ARG V=1

FROM base AS a
RUN echo "a=$V"

FROM alpine AS b
RUN echo "b=$V"
```

options.text: `a=1` and `b=1`, because ARG values are global once declared
options.why: Unrelated stages do not see an ARG declared in another stage.

options.text: `a=1` and `b=`
options.why: Stage `a` is based on `base` and inherits its ARG; stage `b` is unrelated.

options.text: `a=` and `b=`, because every stage needs its own ARG line
options.why: Stages based on a stage that declares the ARG inherit it.

options.text: The build fails at stage `b` with an undefined-variable error
options.why: An undefined variable simply expands to an empty string.

explanation: An `ARG` declared inside a stage is inherited by stages built `FROM` that stage, so `a` prints `a=1`. Stage `b` starts from `alpine`, not `base`, so it has no access to `V`, and an unset variable expands to an empty string. To share a value with unrelated stages, declare `ARG V` in each.

stem:
Why is the `syntax` line here ignored, so the build uses the builder's default frontend?

```dockerfile
# Build image for the API
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22
```

options.text: The `syntax` value must be a full digest, not a tag
options.why: Tags such as `docker/dockerfile:1` are the documented norm.

options.text: Parser directives only work with the legacy builder
options.why: The syntax directive is a BuildKit feature.

options.text: It follows a normal comment, so it is treated as a comment
options.why: Parser directives must appear before any comment, blank line or instruction.

options.text: Directive names are case-sensitive and must be written `SYNTAX`
options.why: Directive keys are case-insensitive and lowercase by convention.

explanation: Once a comment, empty line or instruction has been processed, BuildKit stops looking for parser directives, and anything shaped like one becomes a plain comment. Put `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` on the very first line, then the descriptive comment.

stem:
The context root contains `README.md`, `README-dev.md`, `README-secret.md` and `notes.md`. Which of them are sent to the builder with this `.dockerignore`?

```text
*.md
!README*.md
README-secret.md
```

options.text: `README.md` and `README-dev.md` only
options.why: The last matching line wins: README-secret.md is excluded again by line 3.

options.text: All three README files, since `!README*.md` re-includes them
options.why: A later line overrides an earlier exception for README-secret.md.

options.text: None of them, because `*.md` is matched first and exceptions are ignored
options.why: Exceptions with `!` re-include files matched earlier.

options.text: Every file, because `!` lines turn the whole file into an allow-list
options.why: `!` only creates exceptions; other patterns still exclude.

explanation: For each file, the last `.dockerignore` line that matches it decides whether it is included. `notes.md` matches only `*.md` and is excluded. `README.md` and `README-dev.md` are re-included by `!README*.md`. `README-secret.md` matches line 3 last, so it is excluded.

stem: A `.dockerignore` contains only the line `*.log`. The context has `app.log` at the root and `logs/today.log` in a folder. Which reach the builder?

options.text: Neither, because `*` matches across directory levels
options.why: In filepath.Match rules `*` never crosses a `/`.

options.text: Only `logs/today.log`; use `**/*.log` to exclude logs at every depth
options.why: Patterns are matched from the context root, so `*.log` only hits root files.

options.text: Only `app.log`, because root files are always sent for the Dockerfile
options.why: Root files are excluded like any other match.

options.text: Both, because `.dockerignore` only applies to directories
options.why: It applies to files and directories alike.

explanation: Patterns use Go `filepath.Match` rules relative to the context root, where `*` does not cross directory separators. `*.log` excludes `app.log` but not `logs/today.log`. Docker adds the special `**` wildcard, so `**/*.log` excludes `.log` files anywhere.

stem: In a Dockerfile, `ENV v=""` sets `v` to an empty string and `u` is never set. Match each expression to the value it expands to.

options.text: x
options.why: Default used

options.text: (empty string)
options.why: Value or empty

options.text: y
options.why: Alternate used

explanation: `${var:-word}` gives `word` when the variable is unset or empty, so `${v:-x}` is `x`. `${var-word}` gives `word` only when the variable is unset, so `${v-x}` keeps the empty value and `${u-x}` is `x`. `${var:+word}` gives `word` only when the variable is set and non-empty, so `${v:+y}` is empty.

stem:
Built with `docker build --build-arg username=what_user .`, which user do the two USER lines set?

```dockerfile
FROM busybox
USER ${username:-some_user}
ARG username
USER $username
```

options.text: `what_user`, then `what_user`
options.why: On line 2 the ARG has not been declared yet.

options.text: Empty, then `what_user`, since undeclared variables are empty
options.why: The `:-` fallback applies on line 2, giving some_user.

options.text: The build fails, because `--build-arg` refers to an ARG declared too late
options.why: Declaring the ARG later is fine; it just applies from that line on.

options.text: `some_user`, then `what_user`
options.why: An ARG only comes into effect from the line it is declared on.

explanation: An `ARG` is only in effect from the line where it is declared. Before that, `$username` is empty, so the fallback gives `some_user`. After `ARG username`, the build-arg value `what_user` is used.

stem: A `HEALTHCHECK` command that exits with code `2` puts the container into the `starting` state while it warms up.

options.text: True
options.why: Only 0 (healthy) and 1 (unhealthy) are meaningful exit codes.

options.text: False
options.why: Exit code 2 is reserved and should not be used.

explanation: A health check reports success with exit code 0 and failure with 1; code 2 is reserved. The `starting` state is set by Docker during `--start-period`, not by an exit code. Scripts should map any error to `exit 1`.

stem:
The package name below is misspelled, so `apt-get install` fails. What happens to the build?

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM debian
RUN <<EOF
apt-get update
apt-get install -y curlx
echo "done"
EOF
```

options.text: It fails, because each heredoc line runs as a separate RUN step
options.why: The heredoc is one script run by one RUN step.

options.text: It succeeds: the script runs in the default shell without `set -e`, and `echo` exits 0
options.why: Only the last command's exit status counts; add `set -e` to stop on errors.

options.text: It fails, because BuildKit always runs heredoc scripts with `set -euo pipefail` added
options.why: No error options are added automatically.

options.text: It succeeds, but only because the legacy builder skips heredoc steps
options.why: Heredocs are a BuildKit feature and do run.

explanation: A heredoc that is the whole command is run as one script in the default shell. A plain shell script continues after a failing command, and its exit status is that of the last command (`echo`), so the step passes. Start the script with `set -e`, as in the docs example, or chain commands with `&&`.

stem: Which three instructions have `$VAR` replaced by the builder itself, using ENV and ARG values, rather than by a shell? (Choose three.)

options.text: `WORKDIR $APP_HOME`
options.why: WORKDIR is on the documented list of instructions with builder-side replacement.

options.text: `COPY $SRC /app/`
options.why: COPY supports environment replacement by the builder.

options.text: `USER $APP_USER`
options.why: USER supports environment replacement by the builder.

options.text: `CMD ["echo", "$GREETING"]`
options.why: Exec-form CMD gets no substitution at all, from the builder or a shell.

options.text: `RUN echo $GREETING`
options.why: Shell-form RUN works, but the shell expands it, not the builder.

options.text: `ENTRYPOINT ["/app/$BIN"]`
options.why: Exec-form ENTRYPOINT is passed through literally.

explanation: The builder performs environment replacement in ADD, COPY, ENV, EXPOSE, FROM, LABEL, STOPSIGNAL, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR and ONBUILD. In RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT, any expansion is done by the shell at run time, so exec forms see the literal `$VAR`.

stem:
The image uses an exec-form entrypoint script, yet the app still ignores `docker stop` and is killed after the timeout. What is the fix?

```dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT ["/docker-entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e
./migrate.sh
"$@"
```

options.text: Switch the ENTRYPOINT to shell form so the shell handles signals
options.why: Shell form makes it worse: the shell still does not forward signals.

options.text: Add `STOPSIGNAL SIGKILL` so the container stops immediately
options.why: That just skips graceful shutdown entirely.

options.text: End the script with `exec "$@"` so node replaces the shell as PID 1
options.why: Without exec, the script's shell stays PID 1 and swallows SIGTERM.

options.text: Move `node server.js` from CMD into the ENTRYPOINT array
options.why: Then the migration script would never run; the signal problem is the shell.

explanation: The script runs as PID 1, and `"$@"` starts node as its child. SIGTERM goes to the shell, which does not pass it on. `exec "$@"` replaces the shell process with node, so node becomes PID 1 and gets the signal directly. Official images use this pattern in their entrypoint scripts.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (ENTRYPOINT, exec in entrypoint scripts)

stem:
Built with `docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.36 .`, what do the two RUN steps print?

```dockerfile
ARG VERSION=latest
FROM busybox:$VERSION AS one
RUN echo "one=$VERSION"

FROM busybox:$VERSION AS two
ARG VERSION
RUN echo "two=$VERSION"
```

options.why: Stage one never re-declares the global ARG, so it cannot read it.

options.text: `one=latest` and `two=1.36`
options.why: Without a re-declaration, stage one sees nothing, not the default.

options.text: `one=` and `two=1.36`
options.why: Only stage two re-declares `ARG VERSION`, picking up the build-arg value.

options.text: `one=` and `two=latest`
options.why: A bare `ARG VERSION` takes the build-arg value when one is passed.

explanation: The global `ARG VERSION` feeds both `FROM` lines, so both stages use `busybox:1.36`. Inside a stage the value is only visible after `ARG VERSION` without a default. Stage one prints an empty value; stage two prints `1.36`, the build-arg value that overrides the global default.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Understand how ARG and FROM interact)

stem:
Image `acme/node-onbuild` was built from the Dockerfile below. When does `npm ci` run, and with which `package*.json` files?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
ONBUILD COPY package*.json ./
ONBUILD RUN npm ci
```

options.text: When `acme/node-onbuild` itself is built, using the package files from its own build context
options.why: ONBUILD only records triggers; nothing runs in the base build.

options.text: Every time a container starts from a child image
options.why: Triggers run at build time, not at container start.

options.text: At the end of each child build, after all the child's own instructions
options.why: Triggers run as if inserted right after the FROM line.

options.text: In each child build, just after its `FROM acme/node-onbuild`, using the child's context
options.why: ONBUILD triggers run in the downstream build's context.

explanation: `ONBUILD` stores trigger instructions in the image metadata. When another Dockerfile uses that image in `FROM`, the triggers run in the downstream build as if inserted right after its `FROM`, using the downstream context. That lets a generic base image copy and install each app's own dependency files.

stem: Which two of these lines are invalid in a Dockerfile? (Choose two.)

options.text: `ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN make`
options.why: Chaining ONBUILD with ONBUILD is not allowed.

options.text: `ONBUILD FROM alpine`
options.why: ONBUILD may not trigger FROM or MAINTAINER.

options.text: `ONBUILD COPY . /src`
options.why: COPY is a normal, allowed trigger.

options.text: `HEALTHCHECK NONE`
options.why: This valid form disables a healthcheck inherited from the base image.

options.text: `STOPSIGNAL 9`
options.why: A numeric signal from the kernel table is allowed.

explanation: `ONBUILD` can wrap most instructions, but not another `ONBUILD`, and it may not trigger `FROM` or `MAINTAINER`. `HEALTHCHECK NONE` is a documented form that turns off an inherited check. `STOPSIGNAL` accepts a name like `SIGQUIT` or a number like `9`.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (ONBUILD limitations, HEALTHCHECK, STOPSIGNAL)

stem:
Which labels does the final image carry?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine AS deps
LABEL stage.deps="yes"

FROM alpine AS final
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1"
COPY --from=deps /etc/os-release /tmp/
```

options.text: Both labels, because COPY --from merges the source stage's metadata
options.why: COPY --from copies files only, never metadata.

options.text: Neither: labels are dropped in multi-stage builds unless added with `docker build --label`
options.why: Labels set in the final stage are kept.

options.text: Only `org.opencontainers.image.version`, plus any labels inherited from `alpine`
options.why: Labels from a stage used only through COPY --from are not included.

options.text: Only `stage.deps`, because the first stage's labels take precedence
options.why: The output image comes from the final stage, not the first.

explanation: Labels are inherited along the `FROM` chain: the final image has its base image's labels plus its own. Labels from a stage that is only referenced via `COPY --from` or `RUN --mount=from=` are not included. To keep them, the final stage must be based on that stage.

stem:
Assuming the first URL serves a file, what paths are created by these two lines?

```dockerfile
ADD https://example.com/downloads/tool /bin1
ADD https://example.com/downloads/tool /bin2/
```

options.text: `/bin1/tool` and `/bin2/tool`
options.why: Without a trailing slash, the destination itself is the file name.

options.text: A file `/bin1`, and a file `/bin2/tool`
options.why: A trailing slash means "directory", so the name is taken from the URL.

options.text: A file `/bin1`, and a file `/bin2`
options.why: With a trailing slash the downloaded file goes inside the directory.

options.text: The second line fails, because the directory `/bin2/` does not exist
options.why: Missing destination directories are created.

explanation: For a URL source, a destination that does not end in `/` becomes the file name, so the download is saved as `/bin1`. A destination ending in `/` is a directory, and the file name comes from the URL path, giving `/bin2/tool`. The URL needs a real path for that to work; `http://example.com` alone does not.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (ADD, adding files from a URL)

stem: A team switches `COPY --from=build /out /app` to `COPY --link --from=build /out /app` in the final stage. Which two benefits does `--link` bring? (Choose two.)

options.text: The copied layer no longer depends on the layers below it in the final stage
options.why: With --link the files go into an independent layer that is merged on top.

options.text: With `--cache-from`, the layer can be reused even if earlier final-stage layers changed
options.why: Rebasing onto a new base image no longer forces this copy to rebuild.

options.text: The files are hard-linked instead of copied, so the image takes no extra space
options.why: The name is about layer linking, not filesystem hard links.

options.text: It keeps file ownership from the build stage instead of resetting it to root
options.why: Ownership is still controlled by `--chown`.

options.text: It makes the `build` stage run in parallel with stages that don't use it
options.why: BuildKit already parallelises independent stages without --link.

explanation: `--link` writes the copied files into their own independent layer, which is then merged on top of the earlier layers. Because the layer no longer depends on what came before, a cached result can be reused with `--cache-from` even when the base image or earlier steps changed. This avoids needless rebuilds in multi-stage pipelines.

stem: On Windows, `C:\path` style paths clash with the default `\` escape character. Which character do you set with the `# escape=` parser directive, as Windows Dockerfiles conventionally do? Type the single character.
explanation: The default escape character is `\`, which is also the Windows path separator. Putting `# escape=`` as the first line makes the backtick the escape and line-continuation character, as in PowerShell, so `\` in paths is taken literally.

stem:
The build is started with `DIRNAME=api docker build .` in a shell where `DIRNAME` is exported. What does `RUN pwd` print?

```dockerfile
FROM alpine
ENV DIRPATH=/path
WORKDIR $DIRPATH/$DIRNAME
RUN pwd
```

options.text: `/path/api`
options.why: Shell environment variables from the client are not visible to the builder.

options.text: `/path/`
options.why: An unknown name is not replaced with an empty string here.

options.text: The build fails, because `$DIRNAME` is undefined
options.why: Undefined names do not fail the build.

options.text: `/path/$DIRNAME`
options.why: WORKDIR only resolves variables set in the Dockerfile.

explanation: The reference uses this exact example: `WORKDIR` can only resolve variables explicitly set in the Dockerfile (here `DIRPATH` via `ENV`). `$DIRNAME` is left as literal text, giving `/path/$DIRNAME`. Pass values with `ARG`/`--build-arg` instead of the client shell environment.

stem: With `ENTRYPOINT ["exec_entry", "p1_entry"]` and the shell-form `CMD exec_cmd p1_cmd`, Docker builds one argument vector for PID 1. Put its elements in order.

options.text: `exec_entry`
`p1_entry`
`/bin/sh`
`exec_cmd p1_cmd`

explanation: Exec-form ENTRYPOINT plus shell-form CMD gives `exec_entry p1_entry /bin/sh -c exec_cmd p1_cmd` (the reference's interaction table): the CMD is wrapped in `/bin/sh -c` and appended as arguments. Usually that is not what you want, so use exec form for CMD whenever ENTRYPOINT is in exec form.
reference: Docker docs: Dockerfile reference (Understand how CMD and ENTRYPOINT interact)

stem: An nginx-based image sets `STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT` for graceful shutdown. Which three statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: `docker stop` sends SIGQUIT instead of the default SIGTERM
options.why: STOPSIGNAL changes the signal docker stop and the daemon use.

options.text: Pressing Ctrl+C in an attached `docker run` still sends SIGINT directly
options.why: STOPSIGNAL doesn't affect signals sent from the keyboard.

options.text: `docker run --stop-signal SIGTERM` overrides it for that container
options.why: The image default can be overridden per container.

options.text: The stop timeout grows to match nginx's graceful shutdown time
options.why: The timeout is set separately with `--stop-timeout` or `docker stop -t`.

options.text: SIGQUIT is also sent to every RUN step when a build is cancelled
options.why: STOPSIGNAL only affects stopping containers.

options.text: It only takes effect if the process runs as root
options.why: Signal delivery to PID 1 does not depend on the user.

explanation: `STOPSIGNAL` sets the signal sent by `docker stop` and by the daemon when it stops a container; the default is SIGTERM. Keyboard shortcuts bypass it, since Ctrl+C sends SIGINT directly. Each container can override it with `--stop-signal` on `docker run` or `docker create`.

stem:
A service takes about 40 s to boot. Its health check fails every probe until then, then passes. Starting with this config, which status sequence does `docker ps` show over the first minute?

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --start-period=60s --start-interval=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -fs http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
```

options.text: `starting`, then `unhealthy` after three failed probes, then `healthy` once it passes
options.why: Failures during the start period do not count toward retries.

options.text: `starting` until the first passing probe at about 40 s, then `healthy`
options.why: Probes run every 5 s in the start period and its failures are ignored.

options.text: `healthy` from the start, because the first probe waits 60 s
options.why: Checks run during the start period, at the start interval.

options.text: `starting` for the full 60 s start period, then `healthy`
options.why: A passing probe ends the start period early.

explanation: During `--start-period`, probes run every `--start-interval` (5 s here) and failures don't count toward `--retries`. The first passing probe marks the container started and `healthy`. From then on, failures count, and probes run every `--interval` (30 s).
